significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish both a form-(iii) behavioral law—refusal for otherwise fixed harmful acts is "better fit by log(N) than by linear-N or by no-N effect"—and a supporting form-(ii) mechanism in which a "log-compressed count component" causally limits scale-sensitive refusal and linearization repairs it. This fixes predictions across unmeasured victim counts and explains a specific failure of the refusal pathway, rather than merely finding another refusal direction; that is materially sharper than the default mechanistic template represented by Arditi et al.'s 2024 "Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction." The branches are determinate and useful: linear or superlinear refusal would rule out scope-insensitive refusal, while a log-shaped curve with an inert magnitude intervention would preserve the phenomenon but reject the proposed mechanism. Topic-substitution check: deleting the log-count law and magnitude mechanism leaves only generic LLM-safety interpretability, which would not earn this score; the increment comes from the predictive scaling relation and causal account.

reach.justification: The named handles are the "continuous refusal-vs-count curve" as an auditing quantity and "Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring" as an intervention; the former can screen a model before release and the latter acts before generation, so both provide ex-ante action windows rather than only post-hoc explanation. After per-model re-extraction, the claimed log-versus-linear relation still predicts the qualitative curve expected on a new aligned model, while the exact magnitude direction and anchoring strength require recalibration; the asserted scope covers aligned LLMs and multiple harmful-act classes, not one prompt configuration. Downstream uptake plausibly includes red-teamers, benchmark authors, and refusal-defense designers—existing frameworks such as HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024) and StrongREJECT (Souly et al., 2024) could operationalize victim-count scaling as a pre-deployment audit axis—but the activation intervention is most directly usable on models with internal access. Topic-substitution check: generic safety interpretability alone supplies neither this count-scaling screen nor the scale-sensitive intervention, so the reach score rests on claim-specific transferable handles.
